title: Coarse-grained lock
points: One lock guards all the shared state, for example a synchronized method or one lock around the whole booking system.
It is simple and hard to get wrong, so it is the default starting point.
The cost is overhead and waiting: threads touching unrelated data still queue behind each other.
trade: Use it when load is moderate (human-triggered) or you cannot partition by resource. Move to fine-grained locks only when profiling shows contention. Versus fine-grained: simpler and no deadlock risk between locks, but lower throughput.
test: Seat booking is used by humans at moderate load and seats are all stored in one shared structure. Which lock granularity do you start with and what is its downside?
answer: A coarse-grained lock: simplest and correct. The downside is that bookings for different seats wait on each other.

questions.question: What is the main drawback of a coarse-grained lock?
options: Threads working on unrelated data still wait for each other
questions.explanation: One lock serializes everything. Deadlock risk is a fine-grained concern, and a single lock can protect many variables.

questions.question: Human-triggered traffic at moderate load, and the data cannot be partitioned by resource. What is the sensible choice?
questions.explanation: The decision tree: multiple variables, low contention, no resource partition leads to a coarse lock. Atomics only fit a single variable.
